model.box: A deliberately reduced, machine-readable representation of system intent, structure, behavior, policy, or evidence that supports reasoning, derivation, or checking, and whose relationship to the implemented or observed system is mechanically maintained.

aspects.lead: The intuition the formal statement rests on
aspects.text: Two senses build toward it. A model is a useful approximation — simplified, but good enough to predict; all models are wrong, some are useful, and fidelity trades against cost. And, as this book uses it, a blueprint: a prescriptive description of a system to be built, which the built system is bound to realize. Prose is too vague to enforce, code too verbose to reason over; a model occupies the useful middle.

Each does gatekeeping work. Deliberately reduced — not the whole codebase. Machine-readable — not ordinary prose. A representation of something named — intent, structure, behavior, policy, or evidence — so not everything structured is a model. Supports an operation — reasoning, derivation, prediction, or checking. Mechanically maintained — a drift gate holds it to the system, which is what separates a MAGE model from a stale diagram.

aspects.lead: Constraint, blueprint, and knowledge base at once
aspects.text: A model handed to an agent is at once a constraint (bounding what may be built), a blueprint (saying what to build), and — because the agent reasons over it — the knowledge base for the artifact under construction.

agent.box: A controllable intelligence capable of independent reasoning over a knowledge base.

aspects.text: Given a set of constraints and a goal, it can devise a means of satisfying the goal without violating the constraints — a raven dropping pebbles to raise the water it cannot otherwise reach.

You can change its environment and the knowledge available to it and it does different things, generally following orders. Controllable means probabilistic guarantees; controlled means perfect ones. That one adjective is why governance is a major part of this book — if agents were controlled, we would not need governance at all.
It genuinely reasons in response to a query — not merely retrieving or pattern-matching stored answers.
The thing it reasons over. For this book, the models are that knowledge base — which is what ties the agent definition to the model definition.

engineering.box: The discipline of developing operable technological artifacts to solve problems, and of analytically identifying and assessing the competing means to those solutions, each with distinct trade-offs.

aspects.text: Engineering produces something that works — a technological artifact, with human operators, that addresses a real problem.

This is what separates the engineer from the technician: if you cannot articulate the trade-offs, you are not engineering. An engineer weighs competing architectures and designs against desired properties.

An engineer can model and predict the outcomes of the decisions they are about to make — from the architecture and design they propose — prior to building. Prediction-before-construction is the engineering move.

book_home_owed.note: Landed: the definition is tagged with an index-def in §2.1 (The Agent Stack) and renders as the blue def-box in the web book + PDF.

software-engineering.box: Software development produces a functioning artifact. Software engineering predictively selects a software artifact according to its desired properties.

aspects.text: Development asks "does it function and meet requirements?" Engineering asks "of the artifacts that would function, which one should we build, given the properties we want?" — and answers before building it.

aspects.lead: Why the book is about software engineering.
aspects.text: Prediction-before-construction, applied to software: choosing the artifact whose properties best serve the goal, not merely one that runs.

book_home_owed.note: Landed: the definition is tagged with an index-def in §2.1 (The Agent Stack) and renders as the blue def-box in the web book + PDF.

structured.box: Said of a model: written in an explicit, declared shape a machine can read and validate — a schema, not prose. The declared structure is what lets a machine hold the system up to the model: read the shape, check it for drift, query it, reason over it, enforce it. Structured subsumes type-checking — a type is one way to declare a shape — and names the broader payoff, analyzability. Prose can be a model; only a structured model can be checked.

aspects.text: The structure is a written-down form — fields, states, relations — that a program can parse without a human in the loop. A type is one way to declare it, and type-checking is the sharpest case; a schema, a state table, or a registry declares a shape just as well. What matters is that the model has a shape, the shape is explicit, and a checker can validate any instance against it.

aspects.lead: On what the shape buys — analyzability.
aspects.text: A machine can do to a structured model what it cannot do to prose: read it, check it against the code and fail the build when they disagree, answer queries from it without re-deriving structure from the source, reason over it, and enforce it — refusing work that diverges. "Structured" was chosen over "typed" precisely because it names this whole span, not the type-check alone.

aspects.lead: Why it is the load-bearing half of the Modeling Thesis.
aspects.text: Prose can be a model — simplified, predictive, even prescriptive. But only a structured model can sit at the apex of the documentation hierarchy, because only a machine-readable description can be the one the machine checks the others against. Every "structured, drift-checked model" in this book leans on the adjective: drop it and the drift gate has nothing to read.

churn.box: The condition in which an increasing share of agent effort is spent rediscovering context, undoing recent changes, repairing regressions, or reconciling inconsistencies rather than advancing the system.

aspects.text: Churn is what you can watch — the velocity decay. Its causes are the three not-knowings: what to build, how to realize it, how to change the system without breaking it. Every technique in the book attacks a cause, never the symptom (the churn-is-symptom claim).

aspects.lead: Why it is the agent-era scaling wall
aspects.text: A team of people slows under Brooks's Law. A fleet does not drown in communication; it churns when the work outgrows what it can hold in view — re-deriving what exists, confidently undoing yesterday's fix. Fixing crowds out building.

book_home_owed.note: Landed: the churn inset in the preface premise carries the index-def tag and renders as the light def-inset. Book-only by design; the landing realizes churn as the bi-churn Big-Idea slot.

compounding.box: The positive dual of churn: the regime in which converting recurring engineering judgment into durable mechanisms accrues engineering capital, so an increasing share of future effort can extend capability rather than re-solve settled problems — for as long as that capital stays fit.

aspects.lead: Read it as compound interest, not risk
aspects.text: Compounding is the return on judgment already spent: each conversion lowers the future cost of change, and the lowered costs stack. The word collides with a term the book already uses with the opposite sign — compounding failure probability, where risk multiplies across a long leap. The vehicle disambiguates: capital that earns interest, not error that snowballs.

aspects.lead: Engineering capital is the stock; bureaucracy is its shadow
aspects.text: Compounding is the flow; engineering capital is what it accrues — coherent, economical, quality-bearing governance that durably lowers recurring judgment while it stays fit. Bureaucracy is accumulation that raises the cost of change without reducing future reasoning, so it never compounds.

The environment grows more capable only while the capital stays fit. Two ways accumulation stops compounding: apparatus pushed past the point of fit (the tower-of-governance band of the churn curve), and capital that outlived its fit. That is why mature adaptation is subtractive — reconcile and retire manage capital depreciation, not merely bad apparatus.

governance-mechanism.box: A repeatable environmental structure that encodes an engineering policy and either constrains an action, detects a violation, requires evidence, or controls admission.

aspects.text: Prevention (a constraint — scopes the action space so the mistake is impossible), detection (a sensor — catches the violation and fails the iteration), evidence (demands the change carry its proof — a provenance stamp, a re-derived result), and admission (decides whether the result may advance — the loop's last door). Prevention and detection are the catalogue's constraint/sensor move axis; package names a bundle.

aspects.lead: A model is not a mechanism until enforced
aspects.text: A structured model on disk aims nobody. The lint that reads it, the gate that checks against it, the generator that derives from it — those are the mechanisms. The model supplies the policy; the mechanism supplies the holding.

A one-off inspection is not a mechanism; a mechanism fires on every subsequent change without anyone remembering it. That repeatability is what lets attention be spent per class of failure instead of per change.

engineered-agent-loop.box: A feedback process in which the environment supplies a modeled state, constrains available actions, measures progress against an explicit criterion, and determines whether the result may advance.

aspects.text: The definition names the four things the engineer shapes: the state exposed to the agent, the action surface available to it, the success criterion it steers by, and the admission rule its output must pass. Nearly everything in the book pulls one of these levers.

aspects.lead: How the levers meet the theses
aspects.text: The modeled state is the Modeling Thesis's lever. The constrained actions, the explicit criterion, and the admission rule are the Alignment Thesis's three. The loop is where the two theses meet the running fleet.
Any agent runs in some loop. This one is distinctive because the environment, not the agent, owns all four levers — which makes agent behavior an engineering surface rather than a hope.

reasoning-horizon.box: The amount of intermediate reasoning state a task requires you to hold at once to carry it to a correct result — a property of the task, not of who reasons, whether a human, an agent, or a later architecture.

aspects.lead: The axis the task modes fork on
aspects.text: One-shot scripting sits at a short horizon: the whole transaction fits in one context window and one sitting. Supervised autonomy is for a long horizon: the reasoning state outruns the working memory that must hold it. Writing a shell script, proving a theorem, debugging a deadlock, and re-architecting a subsystem sit at very different points on it.

aspects.lead: Why the constraint is capacity, not a token buffer
aspects.text: A context window instantiates the limit today, but the horizon is architecture-independent: a longer window, a new memory architecture, or a post-transformer system each moves the wall without removing it, because a finite reasoner still has a finite reasoning horizon. This is offered as an analytic generalization for the reader to test, not a measured law.

book_home_owed.note: Landed: the term's index-def anchor lives in §1.3 The Reasoning Horizon, the chapter that develops it (relocated from §1.1 when the Task-Mode fork moved to Part IV §4.1). Book-only by design; the modeling-thesis reframe (§1.4) is where the causal chain it names is worked out.

long-horizon-task.box: A task whose required intermediate reasoning state cannot be held losslessly within the available working memory, so completing it forces compression and reconstruction of that state, at some cost in fidelity.

aspects.lead: Why the lossy round trip matters
aspects.text: When the state will not fit, the reasoner must compress it and rebuild it later, and every lossy round trip degrades the reasoning it stands in for. That degradation is what surfaces as churn — effort spent rebuilding a picture the reasoner keeps losing rather than advancing the system.

aspects.lead: The task class supervised autonomy is for
aspects.text: A long-horizon task is the downward branch of the task-mode fork: too large to hold in a single context window or trust to a single pass. It is why the book spends its weight on supervised autonomy — the method that supplies correctness conditions, tools, and monitoring rather than hoping a single pass lands.

models-bridge.box: The governed channel between the code and the authored system models: the traceability edges that connect model elements to the code they represent, plus the drift checks that hold the two in agreement — the path by which authored models reach the agent's task context and its checks, and the relationship the agent reasons across.

aspects.lead: Map, territory, and the span between them
aspects.text: The authored models are the map; the running code is the territory. The bridge is neither endpoint but the span: the edges a tool can follow from a modeled element to the live symbol it governs, and the gate that fails the build when the two fall out of step. A context-bounded fleet governs a context-exceeding codebase THROUGH this span — it reasons across the bridge, not over the whole territory at once.

Two directions of traffic. Inbound: the models hand the agent the priors its training never gave it — the invariants and intent written where it will read them, instead of guessed from the wrong reference class. Outbound: the drift checks read the code back against the models and redden when a change makes the map lie. The catalogue's models-bridge role is this channel made concrete.

The span is kept as one derived source, re-resolved from live code, not a hand-updated copy that drifts between runs — derived defends, snapshotted drifts. That freshness-by-derivation is a property the bridge has, not the whole of it: the bridge is the traceability-plus-drift relationship; keeping it derived is how it stays honest.
